lead: This unit teaches how stress and strain change when you turn the plane you look at. You will find principal stresses and strains, draw Mohr's circle, read strain rosettes, and choose a failure theory for a loaded part.
about: The unit starts with 2.1, which names uniaxial, biaxial and triaxial stress states and the stress tensor. Chapter 2.2 uses equilibrium of a wedge to get normal and shear stress on an inclined plane; 2.3 writes the same idea as plane stress transformation equations. Chapter 2.4 finds principal stresses, principal planes and maximum shear, and 2.5 shows the same results on Mohr's circle. Chapter 2.6 moves from stress to strain transformation and principal strains; 2.7 applies this to strain gauges and rosettes. Chapter 2.8 compares Rankine, Tresca and von Mises failure theories with factor of safety. Chapter 2.9 closes with equilibrium equations and strain-displacement relations that underpin the whole unit.

chapters.idea: A stress state is fixed by normal and shear components on three faces, and its simplest labels are uniaxial, biaxial and triaxial.
chapters.depth: Define stress at a point as a tensor with six independent components for equilibrium: σx, σy, σz normal and τxy, τyz, τzx shear. Show uniaxial (one normal stress), biaxial (two, plane stress σz=0), triaxial (three). Distinguish plane stress from plane strain; state that plane strain has εz=0, not σz=0. Treat spherical (hydrostatic) and deviatoric parts as advanced; only a few universities teach this split.

figure.title: Stress state split
figure.aria: A flow from the given stresses to a biaxial label, then to mean stress, spherical part and deviatoric part.

chapters.example: At a point, σx=120 MPa, σy=60 MPa, σz=0 and all shear stresses are zero. Name the stress state and split the tensor into spherical and deviatoric parts.
chapters.trap: Calling any two-dimensional drawing plane stress when the problem says plane strain; or thinking σz=0 in plane strain.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: normal and shear stress, Hooke's law, Poisson's ratio.
chapters.leave: Principal values to 2.4; strain transformation to 2.6.

chapters.idea: On a plane tilted by θ, the normal and shear stresses follow from force equilibrium and vary with 2θ.
chapters.depth: Derive σn and τnt on a plane at angle θ by a wedge or by resolving forces. Cover uniaxial and biaxial stress fields, sign convention for θ and shear. Use σn = (σx+σy)/2 + (σx−σy)/2 cos2θ + τxy sin2θ and τnt = −(σx−σy)/2 sin2θ + τxy cos2θ; state that θ is measured from the x face. Some syllabi call τnt the shear stress on the inclined plane.

figure.title: Normal and shear stress vs angle
figure.aria: Two curves show normal stress and shear stress on a plane as the angle theta moves from 0 to 90 degrees.

chapters.example: A plane stress state has σx=80 MPa, σy=40 MPa and τxy=30 MPa. Find the normal stress σn and shear stress τnt on a plane at θ=30° from the x face.
chapters.trap: Using 2θ as the angle in the wedge; or taking θ from the y face instead of the x face.

chapters.idea: Plane stress transformation is a rotation of the stress tensor, and the sum of normal stresses stays fixed.
chapters.depth: Write transformation as matrix rotation of the plane stress tensor. Cover σx′, σy′, τx′y′ equations, invariant σx+σy, and the fact that principal stresses are eigenvalues. Stop before solving principal angles in detail; 2.4 does that. Note plane strain transformation uses ε and γ/2.

figure.title: Stress components in MPa: σx, σy, τxy
figure.aria: An array compares original stress components with components after a 45 degree rotation and shows the unchanged normal-stress sum.

chapters.example: A plane stress state has σx=100 MPa, σy=20 MPa and τxy=40 MPa. Rotate axes by θ=45°. Find σx′, σy′, τx′y′ and check the invariant.
chapters.trap: Forgetting that τx′y′ changes sign with the chosen positive shear convention; or adding 2θ instead of θ in the equations.
chapters.leave: Principal angles to 2.4; strain transformation to 2.6.

chapters.idea: Principal planes carry no shear, and the largest in-plane shear lies halfway between them.
chapters.depth: Derive σ1,2 = (σx+σy)/2 ± sqrt(((σx−σy)/2)² + τxy²), tan2θp = 2τxy/(σx−σy), and τmax = sqrt(((σx−σy)/2)² + τxy²). Cover principal planes 90° apart, maximum shear plane at 45° to principal planes, and absolute maximum shear in 3D with σ3=0. Mention 3D principal directions only briefly; only a few universities solve the cubic.

figure.title: Principal stress route
figure.aria: A flow from given stresses to centre and radius, then to principal stresses and to principal angle with maximum shear.

chapters.example: A plane stress point has σx=80 MPa, σy=-40 MPa and τxy=50 MPa. Find σ1, σ2, θp and the maximum in-plane shear stress.
chapters.trap: Sorting principal stresses incorrectly in 3D; using τmax=R when the absolute maximum shear involves σ3=0.
chapters.leave: Mohr's circle reading to 2.5; yield surfaces to 2.8.

chapters.idea: Mohr's circle turns the transformation equations into one circle whose centre and radius give all plane stress results.
chapters.depth: Construct Mohr's circle with centre C=((σx+σy)/2, 0) and radius R. Plot point A(σx, τxy) and B(σy, −τxy); read principal stresses, maximum shear and principal angle. Cover sign convention and the pole method only if taught; only a few universities use the pole. Do not re-derive transformation equations.

figure.title: Mohr's circle for σx=80, σy=-40, τxy=50 MPa
figure.aria: A circle centred at 20 MPa with radius 78.10 MPa, marked with the two stress points, principal stresses and maximum shear points.

chapters.example: For σx=80 MPa, σy=-40 MPa and τxy=50 MPa, draw Mohr's circle and read σ1, σ2, τmax and the angle from the x face to the major principal plane.
chapters.trap: Plotting both points with the same shear sign, so the circle diameter is wrong.
chapters.prereq: 2.2 to 2.4; coordinate geometry of a circle.

chapters.idea: Strains transform like stresses, but the shear strain term enters as γ/2.
chapters.depth: Define the strain tensor and engineering shear strain γxy. Give transformation for εx′, εy′ and γx′y′/2. Find principal strains ε1,2 = average ± sqrt(((εx−εy)/2)² + (γxy/2)²), principal shear strain, and relation to principal stresses through Hooke's law in 3D. Cover plane strain as εz=0. State that strain gauges measure engineering shear.

figure.title: Strain vs angle
figure.aria: Two curves show normal strain and half the shear strain as the angle theta moves from 0 to 90 degrees.

chapters.example: A plane strain state has εx=400×10⁻⁶, εy=-200×10⁻⁶ and γxy=300×10⁻⁶. Find the principal strains and the principal strain direction.
chapters.trap: Using γxy instead of γxy/2 in the radius; or mixing microstrain with strain.

chapters.idea: Three strain gauges at known angles give the three plane strain components, from which principal strains follow.
chapters.depth: Explain the electrical resistance strain gauge, gauge factor GF=(ΔR/R)/ε, quarter bridge and temperature compensation. Cover rectangular (0°, 45°, 90°) and delta (0°, 60°, 120°) rosettes. Derive εx, εy and γxy from three readings and then principal strains. Only a few universities derive bridge circuits; keep to gauge factor.

figure.title: Rectangular rosette reduction
figure.aria: A flow from three rosette readings to normal strains, shear strain, principal strains and principal direction.

chapters.example: A rectangular rosette reads ε0=500×10⁻⁶, ε45=350×10⁻⁶ and ε90=100×10⁻⁶. Find εx, εy, γxy and the principal strains.
chapters.trap: Forgetting the factor 2 in γxy=2ε45−εx−εy; or using degrees inside the rosette equations without converting consistently.
chapters.leave: Bridge electronics to an instrumentation course.

chapters.idea: A failure theory compares a calculated stress measure with yield strength to get a factor of safety.
chapters.depth: Define yield strength σY and factor of safety FS. Rankine: σ1 ≤ σY/FS for brittle materials. Tresca: σ1−σ3 ≤ σY/FS, maximum shear = σY/2. von Mises: sqrt(0.5[(σ1−σ2)²+(σ2−σ3)²+(σ3−σ1)²]) ≤ σY/FS for ductile materials. Compare yield surfaces in plane stress; hydrostatic stress does not cause von Mises yield. Use principal stresses from 2.4.

figure.title: Failure theory comparison
figure.aria: A flow from given stresses to sorted principal stresses, then to factors of safety by Rankine, Tresca and von Mises.

chapters.example: A plane stress point has σx=100 MPa, σy=-50 MPa and τxy=40 MPa. Yield strength is σY=250 MPa. Find principal stresses and the factor of safety by Rankine, Tresca and von Mises.
chapters.trap: Using σx and σy directly in Tresca or von Mises instead of principal stresses; or forgetting σ3=0.
chapters.prereq: 2.4; Unit 1 factor of safety and material properties.
chapters.leave: Fatigue, fracture and creep to later courses.

chapters.idea: Equilibrium links stress gradients, and strain comes from gradients of displacement.
chapters.depth: Write 3D equilibrium without body forces: ∂σx/∂x + ∂τxy/∂y + ∂τxz/∂z = 0, with two cyclic forms; add body-force terms X, Y, Z if included. Define strain-displacement εx=∂u/∂x, εy=∂v/∂y, γxy=∂u/∂y + ∂v/∂x. Mention compatibility as advanced; only a few universities derive it. Connect to plane stress and plane strain boundary value problems.

figure.title: Displacement to strain
figure.aria: A flow from a displacement field to partial derivatives, then to shear strain and the strain values at point 2 comma 1.

chapters.example: A displacement field is u=(3x+1.5y)×10⁻³ mm and v=(1.5x+2y)×10⁻³ mm, with x and y in mm. Find εx, εy and γxy at (2,1) mm.
chapters.trap: Forgetting that γxy has two derivative terms; or mixing units of displacement and length.
chapters.leave: Compatibility and boundary value solutions to advanced elasticity; beam deflection to Unit 5.
